cards.b: Thin-skinned black grape, cool to moderate climate. Pale to medium colour, high acidity, low to medium tannins, red fruit (strawberry, raspberry, red cherry). Ages to forest floor and mushroom.
Black grape, moderate to warm climate. Medium acidity and tannins. Just ripe: red fruit and green bell pepper. Riper: cooked black fruit, fuller body. Ages to dried fruit and tobacco.
Thick-skinned black grape needing a long warm season. Deep colour, high acidity, high tannins, blackcurrant, black cherry, mint or green bell pepper. Ages to dried fruit, earth, forest floor.

Thick-skinned black grape, moderate to warm climate. Medium to high tannin and acidity, black fruit, black pepper. Moderate: medium body, fresh fruit, herbs. Warm: full body, cooked black fruit, liquorice.
White grape for cool, moderate and warm climates. Cool: apple, lemon, wet stones, high acid. Moderate: lemon, peach, melon. Warm: peach, pineapple, banana, full body. Often shows MLC, lees or oak.
Aromatic white, cool to moderate climate. Dry, high acidity, herbaceous (grass, green bell pepper, asparagus) and blossom; apple and gooseberry to passion fruit. Usually unoaked, drink young.
Aromatic white, cool to moderate climate. High acidity, pronounced fruit and floral aromas. Dry to sweet. Just ripe: apple, lime. Riper: peach, apricot, mango. Ages to honey and petrol.
Same white grape. High-yield, early-picked: dry, light, high acid, apple and lemon (Italian style). Low-yield, late-picked: full body, medium acid, peach, mango, ginger (Alsace style).

cards.f: Côte de Nuits: which red villages?
cards.b: Gevrey-Chambertin and Nuits-Saint-Georges. Northern half of the Côte d'Or, Burgundy. Pinot Noir.

cards.f: Côte de Beaune: which red villages?
cards.b: Beaune and Pommard. Southern half of the Côte d'Or, Burgundy. Pinot Noir.
Regional appellation covering all Burgundy. Light to medium body, low tannin, high acidity, fresh red fruit. Drink young.

cards.f: Burgundy: Premier Cru vs Grand Cru
cards.b: Premier Cru: high-quality vineyards within a village appellation, named with the village. Grand Cru: the very best vineyards, with their own appellations. The most concentrated and age-worthy.
New Zealand. Pinot Noir: the country's ripest and most powerful. Mountains block sea breezes and rain; sunny days, cool nights.
New Zealand, cool to moderate. Very good to outstanding Pinot Noir.
Chile, coastal, cooled by sea breezes and morning fog. Pinot Noir (cooked strawberry), Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc.
South Africa, cooled by strong southerly sea breezes. Pinot Noir with vibrant red fruit; very good Chardonnay.
Victoria, Australia, cooled by the Southern Ocean. Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
Victoria, Australia, cooled by Southern Ocean breezes. Pinot Noir, light and fragrant to riper.
California, cooled by morning fog from San Pablo Bay. Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
California's Central Coast, cooled by sea breezes funnelled inland. Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
USA, cooler than California, mostly moderate. Very good to outstanding Pinot Noir; also Chardonnay with high acidity.
Bordeaux Right Bank. Merlot-dominated blends: full body, black fruit, oak, age to dried fruit and tobacco. Saint-Émilion Grand Cru is a stricter appellation within Saint-Émilion.

cards.f: Bordeaux AOC vs Bordeaux Supérieur AOC
cards.b: Both from anywhere in Bordeaux, usually Merlot-led. Supérieur has slightly stricter rules on yields, ageing and minimum alcohol.
New Zealand North Island, moderate and rainy. Merlot, often blended with Cabernet Sauvignon; full-bodied Chardonnay.
South Africa, mountainous, moderate to warm. Complex Bordeaux varieties: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon.
PGI covering the South of France. Single-varietal Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc.
Bordeaux Left Bank, gravel soils. Cabernet Sauvignon-dominated blends with Merlot. Margaux and Pauillac sit inside the Haut-Médoc.
Left Bank, south of Bordeaux city. Cabernet-led reds; whites blending Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon. Pessac-Léognan is inside Graves.
Napa Valley sub-regions. Full-bodied Cabernet Sauvignon with ripe black fruit and high ripe tannin. Calistoga, in the far north, is warmest.
South Australia, cooled by cloud and southerly breezes. Cabernet Sauvignon with mint, pronounced blackcurrant, smoke and cedar.
Western Australia, warm but cooled by sea breezes. Cabernet Sauvignon (often with Merlot), Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc blended with Semillon.
Chile, within the Central Valley. Cabernet Sauvignon (Chile's most planted grape); foothill sites give mint and green bell pepper.
An estate or producer. The wine was made from grapes grown on the producer's own land.
Bordeaux châteaux ranked in a classification. Among the most expensive Bordeaux; can age for decades.
Médoc wines outside the Grand Cru Classé ranking that can apply for this term. Usually cheaper; some very good to outstanding.
Northern Rhône, far north. Very steep slopes. Complex, peppery Syrah, sometimes co-fermented with a little Viognier.
Northern Rhône. One steep south-facing hill. High-quality, intense Syrah.
Northern Rhône. Larger, flatter area around Hermitage. Less intense Syrah, lower prices.
South of France (Languedoc-Roussillon). Blends including Syrah and Grenache.
South Australia, warm. Very old vines: full body, high ripe tannin, cooked black fruit, pepper, oak (vanilla, coffee).
New South Wales, warm but cloudy with sea breezes. Medium-bodied Shiraz, fresh black fruit; earth and meat with age.
Very broad GI. Inexpensive high-volume Shiraz and Chardonnay, mostly from warm, irrigated inland vineyards.
Northern Burgundy, cool. Dry Chardonnay, high acidity, apple, lemon, wet stones, usually no oak. Frost risk. Premier and Grand Cru on south-facing slopes.
Côte de Beaune villages, moderate. Chardonnay fermented or matured in oak with lees; the best age to hazelnut and mushroom.
Mâconnais, southern Burgundy. Fruity, mostly unoaked Chardonnay: lemon, peach, melon.
Mâconnais, sun-trap slopes. Concentrated stone and tropical fruit Chardonnay, often oaked. Not Pouilly-Fumé (Loire)!
South Australia, cooled by altitude. Chardonnay (ripe peach, medium to high acid); most planted grape is Sauvignon Blanc.
California, warmer further north. Full-bodied Chardonnay with tropical fruit plus vanilla and spice from new oak.
California, coastal parts cooled by Pacific breezes. Pinot Noir and Chardonnay; warmer inland areas for Cabernet and Merlot.
South Africa's broad region. Hot inland vineyards for high-volume Chardonnay, sometimes blended with Chenin Blanc.
Loire Valley, cool, facing each other across the river. Dry Sauvignon Blanc: high acidity, apple, grass, asparagus, wet stones.
Loire, west of Sancerre. Fruity, inexpensive Sauvignon Blanc.
Top of New Zealand's South Island, cool to moderate. Pronounced Sauvignon Blanc: lemon, peach, passion fruit, green bell pepper, asparagus. Also Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
South Africa, cooled by altitude; often called the country's coolest. Sauvignon Blanc with green apple and wet stones.
South Africa, south of Cape Town, cooled by Southern Ocean breezes. Refreshing Sauvignon Blanc with tropical and herbaceous notes.
Germany, northerly. Light-bodied Riesling, often medium-sweet with very high acidity. Steep slopes above the river.
Germany, south-facing slopes on the north bank of the Rhine. Riesling drier and fuller than Mosel.
Germany, near France, sheltered by mountains. Dry, medium-bodied Riesling, similar to Alsace.
South Australia, moderate thanks to altitude. Dry Riesling: lime, peach, blossom, petrol.
France, east of the Vosges, dry and sunny. Wines labelled by grape: dry Riesling, riper Pinot Gris, Gewurztraminer.
Lightest Prädikat. Light body, green apple, lime, blossom. May be dry or have some sweetness.
Prädikat: 'late harvest'. More concentrated and fuller than Kabinett; riper citrus, some peach.
Prädikat: selected extra-ripe bunches. Apricot, mango, dried fruit. Usually some sweetness, can be trocken.
Prädikat: selected botrytis-concentrated bunches or berries. Sweet: apricot, mango, dried fruit, honey.
Prädikat: individually selected berries dried by botrytis. Rare, sweet, even more intense than BA.
Prädikat: grapes frozen on the vine. Fresh peach, apricot, mango; no botrytis. Rare and expensive.
Trocken = dry. Halbtrocken = has some sweetness.
Landwein: German PGI. Qualitätswein: PDO from one of 13 regions. Prädikatswein: PDO needing riper grapes from a single region, in six categories.
North-east Italy. High-volume, inexpensive, light Pinot Grigio.
Italy's north-east corner. More complex, fuller-bodied Pinot Grigio.
Alsace only. Late harvest: usually medium to sweet, from extra-ripe Riesling, Pinot Gris or Gewurztraminer.
Specific vineyards on steep east/south-east slopes of the Vosges. Riper, fuller Riesling, Pinot Gris, Gewurztraminer.
